title: Neonatal & infantile acne
summary: Neonatal acne (birth to 6 weeks) is common and harmless. Infantile acne (6 weeks to about 16 months) can scar and may need treatment. Mid-childhood acne needs an endocrine review.

glance.think: Facial papules and pustules in a baby. Comedones point to true acne; pustules without comedones suggest cephalic pustulosis.
glance.engine: Sebaceous glands driven by maternal and neonatal androgens, plus Cutibacterium.
glance.backbone: Neonatal: observe and cleanse gently. Infantile: BPO ± topical retinoid. No tetracyclines under 12.
glance.never_miss: Acne between ages 1 and 6, signs of hyperandrogenism, or nodular or scarring disease. Refer.

head: Type
Age
Features
rows: Common (about 20% of newborns); facial papules and pustules ± comedones; usually no scarring
Rarer; comedones, papules, pustules, occasional nodules; **may scar**; boys more than girls
Facial pustules **without true comedones**, often linked to *Malassezia*

cause: Overactive sebaceous glands respond to **maternal and neonatal androgens**, with follicular *Cutibacterium* colonisation and the same plugging and inflammation cascade as later acne. Androgen drive falls after infancy and rises again at adrenarche, which is why **mid-childhood acne (ages 1–6) is very rare** and suggests an endocrine cause.

list: **Neonatal:** comedones on the scalp, chest and back; inflammatory lesions on the cheeks, chin and forehead.
**Infantile:** mainly the cheeks; can be more inflammatory or nodular.

diagnosis: Clinical. If the age is atypical or the disease severe, look for accelerated growth, early sexual development or hirsutism. Refer mid-childhood or severe unresponsive acne to endocrinology.

head: Look-alike
Distinguishing clues
rows: No or few comedones; sometimes responds to topical antifungal
Around the mouth and eyes; often steroid-related

management: Usually **observe**. Gentle cleansing; avoid greasy, comedogenic products. Most cases clear without scarring.

list: **Mild:** benzoyl peroxide ± topical retinoid (adapalene or tretinoin) as tolerated. Check the age licence.
**Moderate:** a topical regimen ± an age-appropriate oral **erythromycin**-class antibiotic. **Avoid tetracyclines under 12.**
**Severe, nodular or scarring:** refer to dermatology. Specialists do use isotretinoin in infants when indicated.

red_flags: Suspected hyperandrogenism (accelerated growth, body odour, pubic hair, clitoromegaly).
Nodular or scarring disease, or treatment failure.
pearls: Reassure parents that neonatal acne is not caused by poor hygiene.
Do not use adult OTC acne kits on infants without checking age licences.
Persistent facial pustules in a neonate: consider cephalic pustulosis rather than true acne.
